subject: URGENT: Your account will be suspended in 24 hours
body:
Dear Student,

We detected unusual activity on your university account. Your account will be suspended within 24 hours unless you verify your password immediately.

Click the link below to keep your access.

Northfield IT Helpdesk
red_flags: Sender domain is northfield-helpdesk.example, not northfield.example
Threat of account suspension
Pressure to act within 24 hours
Asks you to verify your password
Link text does not match the real destination
explanation: Real IT departments do not ask for your password by email. The sender's domain only imitates the university's, and the message uses a threat and a deadline to rush you.

subject: CS101: Lecture moved to Room 204
body:
Hi everyone,

This Thursday's lecture will be in Room 204 instead of Room 110. Same time, 10:00 AM. Please bring your laptops for the lab exercise.

See you there,
Prof. Martinez
explanation: Trusted university domain, no links, no requests for information or money, and no pressure. This is a normal class announcement.

subject: You've won a $500 gift card!
body:
Congratulations! You have won a $500 gift card. To claim your prize within 24 hours, pay a small $5 shipping fee using the link below.

Don't miss out!
red_flags: You never entered a contest
Prize requires you to pay a fee
Shortened link hides the destination
Deadline pressure
explanation: Genuine prizes never ask you to pay first. The shortened link hides where you would really land, and the 24-hour limit is there to stop you thinking.

subject: Library hours extended during finals
body:
Hello,

To help you study, the main library will stay open until 2:00 AM from December 5 to December 16. Quiet study rooms can be booked on the library website.
explanation: The sender and the link are both on the university's own domain, and the message only gives information. Nothing is being asked of you.

subject: Textbooks up to 60% off - this week only!
body: Save big on required textbooks. Prices drop this week only. Browse the full catalogue below.
red_flags: Name says 'Campus' but the domain is not the university's
'This week only' sales pressure
explanation: It is not clearly malicious, but it uses a campus-sounding name from an outside domain. Check the official bookstore website directly instead of using the email's link.

subject: Complete a 2-minute survey for a coffee voucher
body:
Dear Student,

Help improve campus life! Finish our short survey and receive a coffee voucher.
red_flags: Official-sounding name from an outside domain
Generic greeting ('Dear Student')
Reward used as bait
explanation: Surveys are a common way to collect personal data. Because the sender is not on the university domain, treat it with caution and confirm with the student office.

subject: Flexible remote assistant job - no experience needed
body:
Hello,

We are hiring students for a remote assistant role. Earn $400 per week working just a few hours. No experience needed. Reply with your phone number and availability and we will send details.
red_flags: Free personal email address for a 'company'
Unrealistic pay for little work
No company details or job description
explanation: Fake job offers target students who need money. Vague roles, high pay and a free mail address are classic signs. Verify real jobs through the university career centre.

subject: You've been selected for a $2,000 scholarship
body:
Congratulations!

You have been selected for the Northfield Excellence Award. To confirm your eligibility, submit your student ID number and date of birth using the form below.
red_flags: Domain northfield-awards.example is not northfield.example
You did not apply
Asks for ID number and date of birth
explanation: Scammers combine the university name with an outside domain and ask for identity details. A real scholarship office would use the official domain and never ask for this by email.

subject: Spring registration opens December 1
body:
Hello,

Spring course registration opens on December 1. Review your registration time in the student portal and register before the December 12 deadline.
explanation: A deadline alone is not a warning sign. The sender and link are both on the university domain, and nothing asks for a password or payment.

subject: Your package could not be delivered
body:
Dear customer,

We tried to deliver your package but no one was home. Confirm your address within 48 hours to reschedule.
red_flags: Generic greeting
Unencrypted http link
Deadline pressure
You may not be expecting a parcel
explanation: Delivery notices are a very common lure. If you are not expecting a parcel, go to the courier's official site yourself rather than using the link.

subject: Update your direct deposit details
body:
Hello,

To make sure your next payment arrives, please provide your bank account number and routing number by replying to this email.
red_flags: The real domain is hr-portal.example (northfield.example is only a prefix)
Asks for bank account details by email
explanation: Read domains from right to left. 'northfield.example' appears at the front, but the address actually ends in hr-portal.example. Payroll changes are made in the official portal.

subject: Meeting this Thursday at 6 PM
body:
Hi members,

We meet Thursday at 6 PM in the Student Union, room 3. Bring a board if you have one. Details are on our club page.
explanation: Trusted domain, a link on the university's own site, and a routine request. Nothing unusual.

subject: Your session has expired
body:
Hello,

For your security your session has expired. Please sign in again to continue using your university services.

Thank you,
Northfield Identity Services
red_flags: The domain has a digit 1 in place of the letter l (northfie1d)
The link text does not match where the link goes
Polished wording hides a fake login page
explanation: No scare tactics here, which is what makes it hard. Zoom in on the domain: 'northfie1d' uses the number 1. The login page it leads to would steal your credentials. Note that the authentication checks all pass: the attacker owns the look-alike domain, so 'pass' only proves the email came from that domain, not that the domain is trustworthy.

subject: Quick favor
body:
Hi,

I'm in a meeting and can't talk. I need 4 gift cards for a department event. Please buy them and reply with the codes. I'll reimburse you.
red_flags: Reply-To goes to a free personal address
Request for gift card codes
Unusual request from someone in authority
explanation: The sender looks real, but replies go to a personal address. Gift-card requests from a 'busy boss' are a well-known scam, either spoofed or sent from a hacked account. The failed SPF/DMARC checks in the headers back this up.

subject: Your aid package has been updated
body:
Hello,

Your financial aid package has been updated for the spring term. Please log in to the student portal to review your award.

Financial Aid Office
explanation: It mentions money and a login, which can feel risky, but the sender and link are both on the university domain and it asks for no information. Not every message about aid is a scam.

subject: Action needed: set up multi-factor authentication
body:
Hello,

All students must register for multi-factor authentication this month. Follow the link below to complete setup.
red_flags: The link uses 'xn--' encoding, which can disguise look-alike letters
Link text and real destination differ
explanation: The sender address looks fine, but the link does not go where it says. Always check the real destination before clicking; if in doubt, open the MFA page by typing the official address. The failed SPF and DMARC checks in the email headers also show it was not really sent by the university.

subject: Invitation: invited speaker at International Symposium
body:
Dear Researcher,

Based on your recent work, we would like to invite you to speak at our symposium. A refundable registration fee of $150 secures your slot. Please see the details on our site.
red_flags: Unsolicited invitation
Asks for a fee up front
No verifiable organisation behind it
explanation: Predatory conferences flatter you and then charge a fee. It may be a scam or just low quality, so check the organisers independently before paying or replying.

subject: Shared a document with you
body: Hey, I shared our group project notes with you. Open the link to take a look.
red_flags: Link leads outside the university to an unknown site
Very short message with no context
explanation: The sender's address is real and every authentication check passes, because the email genuinely came from Alex's account. That is exactly why a hacked account is dangerous. An unexpected link to an unknown site deserves a quick check with Alex through another channel. The rule-based detector often misses this one.

subject: Your student loan qualifies for 100% forgiveness
body:
Congratulations!

Your federal student loan has been approved for full forgiveness. To finalize, confirm your date of birth and bank account details within 48 hours or your approval will be cancelled.
red_flags: Official-sounding name but an unrelated outside domain
Too-good-to-be-true offer
Asks for date of birth and bank details
48-hour deadline
explanation: Real loan servicers do not announce forgiveness by email and never ask for bank details to 'finalize' it. Loan relief is a popular lure for students; check your loan servicer's official site yourself.

subject: You have a tuition refund of $842 waiting
body:
Hello,

A refund of $842 is available for your account. To receive it, confirm your bank account number using the secure form below.
red_flags: Domain is northfeld.example, missing the letter 'i'
Asks for a bank account number
Link goes to the same look-alike domain
explanation: One missing letter turns northfield.example into northfeld.example. Refunds are handled inside the official student portal, not through a form sent by email.

subject: Room selection closes tonight!
body:
Hi,

Room selection for next year closes tonight. Choose your room now through the link below before the best rooms are gone.
red_flags: Official-sounding name from a non-university domain
Pressure to act tonight
explanation: Housing deadlines are a real worry for students, which scammers exploit. Check the dates in the official housing portal rather than trusting an outside domain.

subject: Unpaid parking violation - $65
body:
Your vehicle has an unpaid parking violation of $65. Scan the QR code below to pay within 24 hours and avoid a late fee.

[ QR CODE IMAGE ]
red_flags: QR code hides the real destination (a shortened http link)
Official-sounding sender on an outside domain
24-hour deadline
explanation: This is 'quishing': QR-code phishing. You cannot read a QR code's destination by eye. Pay parking fines through the official campus website, and be wary of QR codes on emails or flyers.

subject: Move-out reminders for winter break
body:
Hello residents,

Residence halls close on December 18 at noon. A checklist for moving out is available on the housing website. Have a great break!
explanation: Trusted university sender, link on the university's own housing site, and no request for money or personal details. It is routine.

subject: Scheduled maintenance on Saturday
body:
Hello,

Email and campus Wi-Fi may be briefly unavailable on Saturday between 2 and 4 AM while we upgrade our systems. No action is needed. Remember, IT will never ask for your password by email.

Northfield IT Services
explanation: The word 'password' appears, but only in a warning. Look at what the email actually asks you to do: nothing. A good rule is to judge the request, not just keywords.
